title: Mary prays (CCC 2617–2619)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus prays: a whole night before choosing the Twelve, thanks before the miracle, not my will but thine. Your line was he prayed first. Did you pause before a choice? Day one thousand one hundred forty.

Two scenes, close together in Luke's Gospel. In the first, a woman in Nazareth hears an angel's message that will rearrange her whole life, and she answers in one sentence. In the second, she has walked into the hill country to see her cousin Elizabeth, and when Elizabeth greets her, she doesn't answer in one sentence. She sings. A short yes, and then a long song. Yesterday, the Catechism showed the Son praying. Today it turns to his mother, and to those two prayers. Mary prays.
screen: `NAZARETH: ONE SENTENCE.` → `THE HILL COUNTRY: A SONG.` → `A SHORT YES, A LONG SONG.`

segments.voice: The first prayer. The angel Gabriel tells Mary she will bear a son. She asks how. He answers. And she says, in the Douay-Rheims, "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word." In Latin, that "be it done" is one word: fiat. The Catechism says simply: this is Christian prayer, to be wholly God's, because he is wholly ours. Notice it isn't a request. It's an offering. She doesn't know what comes next, and she says yes anyway. Then the second prayer. Mary visits Elizabeth, who calls her blessed. And Mary answers: "My soul doth magnify the Lord. And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." In Latin it begins Magnificat, and that's what the song is called. The Catechism calls it the song both of the Mother of God and of the Church. It goes on to sing that God has scattered the proud, put down the mighty, lifted up the lowly, and filled the hungry with good things. Praise, in Mary's mouth, is not polite. It's a song about the world turned right side up. The Catechism points to one more moment. At a wedding in Cana, when the wine runs out, Mary tells Jesus, and then tells the servants, "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." The Catechism sees her there as one who asks on behalf of others, and points them toward her Son. So the shape of Mary's prayer, as the Catechism draws it: first, yes. Then, praise. And all along, pointing past herself.
screen: `BE IT DONE TO ME: FIAT.` · `WHOLLY GOD'S.` · `MY SOUL DOTH MAGNIFY THE LORD.` · `WHATSOEVER HE SHALL SAY TO YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray yes, then praise. Settle, and breathe. First, the yes. Bring to mind one thing you've been resisting, something you can't control. Without solving it, try letting it be. If you pray, you can borrow Mary's words, be it done to me according to thy word. Then the praise. Name, slowly, a few good things that are real today. If you pray, you can offer them up, the way the Magnificat does. If you don't, just let yes and gladness sit side by side. The bell holds the time.
Mary prays. Her fiat at the Annunciation, be it done to me, and her Magnificat at the Visitation, my soul doth magnify the Lord: in Catholic teaching, yes to God, then praise. Today's word.
Your line: yes, then praise. Today, when something lands on you that you didn't choose, try the yes first, and look for one thing to praise after. Day one thousand one hundred forty.

howItsDone: Catholics say Mary's fiat in the Angelus, where be it done unto me according to thy word is one of its lines, and the Magnificat is sung or said at Vespers, the evening prayer of the Liturgy of the Hours.

original.note: Latin: let it be done — Mary's answer in Luke 1:38, in the Vulgate.

trapdoor: what you thought: Mary is someone Catholics ask for prayers, not someone shown praying.
what it means: the Gospel shows Mary praying: her yes to God, and her song of praise.
what a scholar hears: fiat, the Latin 'be it done' of Luke 1:38, and Magnificat, the opening word of Luke 1:46's song, which the Catechism calls the song of the Church.

notes: CCC 2617–2619 paraphrased (copyrighted translation). Check: the fiat as Christian prayer in its purest form, 'to be wholly his, because he is wholly ours' (2617); Cana (2618); the Magnificat as the song of the Mother of God and of the Church (2619).
Fiat and Magnificat are Vulgate words ('fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum', 'Magnificat anima mea Dominum'); confirm.
howItsDone: the Magnificat at Vespers is standard in the Liturgy of the Hours; confirm 'every evening' phrasing.
Douay-Rheims Luke 1:38, 1:46–47, John 2:5: confirm exact wording.
Editor: 'Christian prayer in its purest form' (not CCC 2617's wording) replaced with 'this is Christian prayer'; unsourced 'young' cut.

Editor (second pass): trapdoor no longer calls fiat the opening word of Luke 1:38 (the Vulgate answer opens 'Ecce ancilla Domini'; fiat comes mid-sentence); howItsDone's 'every evening' claim softened.

Audit (1132–1141 pass): howItsDone said Catholics pray Mary's words 'in the rosary'; the Hail Mary is Gabriel's and Elizabeth's words to Mary, not hers, so the rosary claim is cut and the Angelus (which does contain 'be it done unto me according to thy word') kept. Luke 1:38, 1:46–47, John 2:5 (Douay-Rheims) and CCC 2617–2619 checked and found accurate.
